speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. P. F. CASGRAIN (Secretary of State):
subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNISTIC ATTITUDE OF CERTAIN FOREIGN-LANGUAGE NEWSPAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the house to a question which was raised on Friday by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) with reference to the alleged communistic attitude of certain foreign-language newspapers.
Both the papers to which Doctor Kirk-connell referred are being constantly watched. Considerable material indirectly suggesting communistic sympathies, if not direct communistic inspiration, has been observed, but conclusive material has been avoided, by accident or otherwise. Each issue of both these weekly papers is closely examined by translators whose reports go to the press censors.
The Hungarian paper, published in Toronto, has been watched closely since the war started. It was quite often openly communistic until the communist party of Canada was declared an illegal organization last June. Since then it has been edited in technical accord with the defence of Canada regulations, although some suspicious material has appeared.
The Ukrainian language paper cited by Doctor Kirkconnell, published in Smoky Lake, Alberta, has a small circulation, confined to its immediate district. It is not as skilfully edited as the Hungarian paper mentioned. It may be said to be on probation at the present time, since a blunt warning was given its editor less than three months ago, February 26th. This warning brought from the editor assurances of future cooperation. Since then he has submitted some material before publication which he was

informed was of questionable legality. Suspicions regarding this paper remain, but it has stayed technically within the law.
The report is signed by the press censors.

maintopic: DETENTION OF EMPLOYEE OF CANADIAN BRO.ADCASTING CORPORATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DETENTION OF EMPLOYEE OF CANADIAN BRO.ADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Last week Mr. James A. Murphy, an employee of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and president of the radio division of the Association of Technical Employees, was in Ottawa negotiating with the Department of Labour for a conciliation board to inquire into a dispute between the corporation and some of its employees. Upon Mr. Murphy's return to Toronto on Friday, and after he had reported for work, he was arrested in the Toronto studio under the defence of Canada regulations, according to the Globe and Mail of Saturday, May 24, 1941. Mr. Murphy's wife was told that she might see her husband on Saturday, but upon presenting herself, was refused an interview. No one, including his lawyer, has been allowed to see him, and no one has been notified of the precise charges against him.
The timing and circumstances surrounding the police action arouses grave suspicion as to the motives governing this arrest. Will the Minister of Justice inform the house of the charges and indicate why, if this man has been suspected of offences against the defence of Canada regulations, the arrest was made during the process of negotiations between the CBC and the union?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DETENTION OF EMPLOYEE OF CANADIAN BRO.ADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member sent me notice of this question, which I desire to answer as follows:
James A. Murphy, an employee of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, has been detained under the provisions of the defence of Canada regulations on the grounds of his communistic activities. He is believed to be a member of the communist party and to have assisted in the construction and supply of the radio equipment used in a motor car on behalf of the communist party by one Parsons, who was recently convicted under the defence of Canada regulations in Toronto.
It was not known in the Department of Justice or to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at the time of issuing the order for detention that Mr. Murphy was negotiating for a conciliation board with the Department of Labour, and, if he was so negotiating, his arrest was merely a coincidence, as at the time of the issuing of the order the Royal Canadian

Excise Tax Act
Mounted Police had merely carried their investigation to the point where it was considered essential that immediate action should be taken, and the negotiations with the Department of Labour did not enter into consideration in any manner.
Under the defence of Canada regulations a detained person, if he objects to his detention, is informed by the advisory committee of the grounds upon which he is detained, and he is further given the privilege of consulting his solicitor. Prior to that time it is not the practice to permit interviews with the detained person. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police did inform Mrs. Murphy that she might see her husband on Saturday, but when she went to the gaol she was not permitted by the gaoler to have this interview, as interviews on Saturday are contrary to the regulations of the gaol. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, however, wrote to the gaoler requesting that Mrs. Murphy be permitted to see her husband to-day, Monday, and that she be not restricted to the usual three-minute interview. It is understood that this arrangement is being carried out.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section	1-Definitions-"Raw	leaf
dealer."

This is
rather technical, and so far as I can recall there was no reference to this proposed enactment in the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

It really
sets up a new authority, if I may so suggest, and I should like to have from the Minister of National Revenue or his colleague a statement as to why the change has been made. Is it an eleventh hour idea? How many of these tobacco packers are there, and what is the present position as to granting licences?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill
is twofold. The part I am dealing with, comprising the first seven sections, places raw leaf tobacco on the same basis as manufactured tobacco. The budget in 1940 placed an excise duty of ten cents a pound on raw leaf tobacco sold for consumption in its natural state, to be collected by means of stamps affixed to the packages. Persons engaged in its preparation for use were required to obtain a licence as raw leaf dealers, at a nominal fee of $2 per annum. There were 4,282 such licences during the period from August, 1940, to March 31, 1941. Considering the small amount of revenue involved and the numerous licencees, it has not proved feasible to provide supervision such as would result in the effective collection of revenue. Fraud and deception have resulted; hence it has been decided to place the processing of Canadian raw leaf tobacco on the same basis as the manufacture of tobacco by charging the same licence fee and requiring that the licencee operate under excise supervision in the same manner as the tobacco manufacturer.
That means that the nominal fee of $2 has been raised to $50?
That is right.

It is a substantial increase. Is it intended that the number of tobacco packers shall be materially reduced, giving them a new designation instead of "raw leaf dealer?" I understood the minister to say that there were over 4,000 of these

Excise Tax Act
dealers. Now they are to be called tobacco packers and simulated to tobacco manufacturers on the basis of $50 instead of $2. Will that not have the effect of eliminating a large number of licensees?
Yes, it will cut down the number so that they can be adequately dealt with and supervised.

Will that not tend towards monopoly? Combines, monopolies, trusts-does that ring in the ears of any hon. members of the house? I heard it in this house for ten years. The minister should give more justification than that. He alleges there has been evasion. I suppose there never was an excise act, a customs act, or indeed any prohibitory legislation-game laws, liquor laws, and other enactments of the kind with which we are surrounded-that was not subject to evasion. But that in itself is not an argument for this change. What I suppose the minister intended to convey by the written memorandum which he read to the committee was that it will be much easier to administer the law and see that the revenues from excise go into the treasury by this method than by the other. That is really what the object of the legislation is, is it not?

Yes. The position is very much as if we tried to collect a tax on the sale of cigarettes from the retailer, leaving it to the retailer himself to stamp each package before he sold it. Under the existing legislation dealers have been able to buy a few stamps and keep them in their shops, and whether they put them on or not was a matter which was very difficult to control. If they were selling to their friends they might not put on the stamps; if they were selling to strangers they might. There has been some leakage, and it was felt that the stamping should be done by some central body such as the packers. Licences will be freely issued to people applying to become packers.

I am glad to have the minister give that assurance. Fifty dollars will be quite a deterrent to the issuing of licences, and I suggest that the fee is too high. It is something that the dealer will have to absorb, and it is being raised from a nominal fee to a revenue fee. What is the justification for the increase? As to the argument made by the minister, on the question of evasion, I suggest that it constitutes a grand attack on the legislation of two of the provinces which have lately put taxes on a commodity that is almost of universal consumption, namely, tobacco. In Quebec and New Brunswick, which have adopted this, shall
(Mr. R. B. Hanson.]
I say, nefarious tax-I am speaking from the point of view of the consumer-they make the retailers collect the tax, and the tax is imposed in the guise of a hospital tax or a TB tax, if you please, when of course it is simply nothing but a revenue measure. It is disguised under the euphemistic name "TB tax." I agree with the minister that it is very difficult to administer that sort of tax. Evasions of the law will be numerous and there is no effective way to check them. The minister's argument of course is in favour of easier administration of the excise act, and to that extent I think it is to be commended.
Having received the minister's assurance that licences will be freely issued, I suggest to him that the only objection there can be to this legislation is the size of the fee for a licence. I ask the minister to justify the raising of the fee from $2 to $50.
This is the same fee as is charged to manufacturers of tobacco, and when these tobacco packers' plants are established we shall have to have an excise officer supervising the work of each.

He has to do that now. That does not mean any new commitments, does it, in the way of extra excise men? A tobacco manufacturer usually does business in large volume. Surely a tobacco packer, if licences are freely issued, will not be doing anything like the volume of business that a tobacco manufacturer does. Therefore a licence fee on the same basis is not justified. The minister is just trying to get a little more revenue; isn't that the idea?
No. There will be some very large packers and there will have to be an official spending his full time in each of these packing establishments, just as in manufacturing plants.

I should like to congratulate the minister on this particular phase of his budget proposals. These raw leaf dealers, I understand, are a detriment to the tobacco trade of Canada, who produce approximately $55,000,000 of excise. I should like to record that.

The minister made some reference to cigarettes, and the leader of the opposition has indicated that the minister may be using the cigarette trade as a means for collecting additional revenue. I should like to know if there is any such plan that has peculiar application to western Canada. I hold in my hand a package of Sweet Caporal cigarettes made by the Imperial Tobacco company. This package contains twenty-two cigarettes. When I was home at Easter

Excise Tax Act
I found that the same package in Saskatchewan contains only twenty cigarettes but is sold at exactly the same price. That represents an increase in price'of 2i cents or 10 per cent in Saskatchewan as compared with Ontario. Is that due to an effort on the part of the government to collect additional revenue, or is it a device on the part of the manufacturer to collect an additional price from the people of Saskatchewan? It cannot be explained by freight, which is the usual excuse advanced by manufacturers for imposing an increased price upon those of us who live in western Canada.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Licence to carry on business of tobacco packer.
On the point of licences again, is this to be one fee for all time, or an annual fee?
It is an annual fee.
The bill does not make it clear.
The reason is that all excise duty licences expire on March 31.

The new section 277 seems to me to be a very large and comprehensive delegation of authority to the minister to make regulations. Is this necessary? I know we are in an age of delegation of authority. Parliament has delegated almost all its powers except that of levying taxation and the provision of ways and means. I am not in a position to say whether this is necessary or not; I do not know enough about the matter. But on the principle involved I want the minister to justify such a large and comprehensive delegation of authority to the minister. Could the regulations not have been put into the statute? I see the commissioner of excise gives a most emphatic "no". Of course he probably knows a good deal more about it than I do. But that little incident illustrates the point that has often been borne in upon me: I wonder if I cannot page some of the members of parliament who have been complaining that the deputy ministers are running the government, not the government running the departments. That remark, however, is made only facetiously; I know the Department of National Revenue is very well administered, but the incident that occurred a moment ago serves to illustrate what has often been said in that regard, not so much by me as by hon. members supporting the government. I note that they are all very quiet in their seats or
have disappeared from the chamber, and that I am not going to get any support on this point. But I would ask the minister to clarify the position. Why is it necessary to delegate these very wide powers to the minister?

We could have put in a blanket section which would carry the same authority. We have here detailed portions of the 'business that will be subject to regulations. The industry changes from time to time, and the requirements change, and the minister, on the advice of his commissioner, who is experienced in the working out of the details, puts the regulations into effect so that the act can be properly administered.
The effect of that statement is that by a system of trial and error the commissioner will finally arrive at a method of government by regulation which he thinks will block up every hole.
We certainly hope to block up every hole.

Let me call the minister's attention to section 6 of the bill, not by way of anticipating that section but by way of comparison. By sections 278, 279 and 280, regulations are embodied in the statute, as distinguished from the delegation of authority to the minister provided for by section 277. The two things do not jibe. Why the one and not the other? Why is the authority taken here and not sought there? It is true they do not deal with exactly the same subject matter, but all of them provide machinery for the enforcement of the law.
How many new excise officers will be required to administer this act, if every packer has to have an excise officer full time?
It is anticipated that we shall use our present staff almost entirely. A few more may be required, depending upon how many licences are necessary, but very few.
In other words there is a full time excise officer on the premises of every tobacco packer in the country now?
I think the hon. member is referring to a dealer.

The one who has to take out the licence. The minister said a full time excise officer would have to be on the premises of each packer. How many additional excise officers will be required to administer that part of the act, or is it possible to put the tobacco in warehouses and simply have an officer check on it from time to time?

At present officers are going around inspecting the tobacco dealers, of whom we have some four thousand. That
Excise Tax Act

is done, of course, with the help of the mounted police. Now, however, if we have all the domestic tobacco going into the hands of the packers, one inspector will be in charge of each plant, instead of having inspectors go around and inspect some four thousand dealers.

That does not indicate, however, how many excise inspectors will be required. How many tobacco dealers will have to have their accounts checked under this new provision? In other words, this is a change, and according to the minister's own statement it will now be necessary to have a full time excise officer at each place. How many places are there, and how large an addition to the staff of the department will be required?

It may not result in any addition at all to the staff. Already we have inspectors going around to the dealers; and if the dealers are eliminated, the inspectors will be in the plants of the packers, who will pay the tax. We cannot estimate how many packers will demand licences. There might be forty or fifty, but as I said before it is not anticipated that there will be any great increase in the staff required.
In the opinion of the department what loss has been sustained by not having had a check on the raw leaf dealers of the dominion? Has any approximate compilation been made in that regard?

No, we have not been able to make any approximation of what has been lost. When we have found the law being evaded of course prosecutions have been instituted, but it is very difficult indeed to estimate what would be the amount of the loss.

Does the minister
anticipate that this legislation will result in holding to a minimum the number of independent raw leaf dealers?
We are not really trying to hold them to any number. We want to be able to supervise them and keep the whole thing under proper jurisdiction and control.

Why under section 4 is the minister given authority to do one thing, while under section 5 he has put the regulations right in the act? In section 277(a) it is provided that the minister may make regulations for causing accounts to be kept by tobacco packers, and so forth. Possibly this would be the proper place for me to discuss a matter I had intended bringing to the attention of the government. On many occasions in the house I have appealed against the importation of potatoes into British Columbia, particularly when we have such a heavy surplus crop. My appeal is now made because under the customs tariff potatoes are permitted to enter British Columbia free of duty from southern United States, with the exception of about six weeks between June 15 and August 7. Only during that short period is there a tariff. British Columbia grows early potatoes, and the potatoes of that province are now on the market. In Vancouver, New Westminster and other points in the province they reached the market on May 23, which is the usual time for our early potatoes to be marketed. No protection is given the growers of early potatoes from importation south of the line, until June 15. My appeal to both ministers, and particularly

to the Minister of National Revenue, is that the date should be changed back, giving our growers a much needed protection.
I am not sure what procedure the Department of National Revenue follows, but I am wondering if its officials call into consultation officials of the Department of Agriculture as to when these dates are to be set. To-day we have in British Columbia a surplus of potatoes, over and above what will be required for normal consumption, of something like 3,000 tons. Yet potatoes grown in southern California-and, by the way, they have had a second crop this year-potatoes grown in irrigated land, on land producing up to twenty tons per acre, are appearing on the British Columbia market in large quantities. Further, the potatoes which are being imported are No. 2 quality, not No. 1; they are somewhat smaller in size. The result is that the early potato growers of British Columbia are being penalized.
I suggest that the date should be set back so as to give our growers more protection which, in my opinion, is required by them. I shall not at this time enter into a tariff argument, but I do appeal to both ministers, on behalf of the potato growers of British Columbia, to set the date back. We have a large surplus of old potatoes which have been kept in splendid condition and are perfectly good. In view of the quantities we have on hand, if a tariff is to be imposed I can see no reason why it should not become effective on May 15 instead of June 15.

'The explanatory note to section 1 reads:
This amendment removes from the profits *subject to the 75 per cent rate of taxation any constructive dividend received by a corporation as a result of the winding-up, discontinuance of 'business, or reorganization of another corporation. In order to prevent this exemption being used as a means of avoiding personal income taxes it is restricted to cases where the corporation receiving the dividend or the corporation paying the dividend is held or controlled by more than twenty-five shareholders.

What is
meant by a constructive dividend in this sense?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A constructive dividend is a distribution of surplus which is deemed to be a dividend for taxation purposes under section 19 of the Income War Tax Act. There are companies which have accumulated income and have an earned surplus. The time may come when they wish to distribute that surplus to their shareholders. That distribution is deemed to be a dividend for taxation purposes; that is, the shareholder is taxed as if it were a dividend and not a distribution of capital. That is what is meant by a constructive dividend. It is not deemed just to tax that constructive dividend at the high rate under the Excess Profits Tax Act. For instance, if corporation B is a shareholder in corporation A and corporation A makes a distribution of earned surplus, it will be seen at once that that might of itself put corporation B in the 75 per cent class. It might mean a very large tax if it were subject to the 75 per cent

rate of taxation. This section is for the purpose of making it clear that it is not so. It would be subject, however, to the 40 per cent rate of taxation, which is exactly what the law intended. That is the corporation income tax rate.
All corporations are paying that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. There are cases where it might be a temptation to a company to get its surplus out at the 40 per cent rate instead of distributing it to the individual shareholders at the personal income tax rates, which might be higher than 40 per cent. That could only be done as a device to avoid individual income tax if there were some degree of control, some relationship between the two corporations. Therefore the concluding provisions of this section are to make sure that in those circumstances the 75 per cent rate will apply, if they are in the 75 per cent class, notwithstanding the first provisions of the section.

Within
certain limitations. Why is the number of shareholders fixed at twenty-five? It is an arbitrary figure, I suppose.

I suppose this is about as good a place as any for me to say what I wish to say with regard to the excess profits tax. I had hoped that the 1940 returns of the thirty-three companies to which I alluded last year might be all available so that one could make a comparison to see how the excess profits tax actually worked out in. practice

Excess Profits Tax Act
during the past year, but unfortunately I have not been able to get them all together. I have been working on a number of 'reports, and I find, taking twenty-eight- of these companies, that after the taxes had been paid for the last year, after income and other taxes had been deducted, of the twenty-eight companies the net income amounted to $124,286,000 as against $132,676,000 for the previous year. This would seem to indicate that even with our excess profits tax, income tax and so on, slightly less net profit was made by these twenty-eight companies, of the thirty-three to which I alluded last year, than in the preceding year.
I realize the difficulty of dealing with the excess profits tax to meet every type of company and every contingency that can arise, and when the final reports are in for the excess profits and other taxes of last year, the Minister of Finance and his officials may be able to come to a better basis and conclusion that we have yet arrived at. However, I am not being carpingly critical of what has been done by the minister up to the present time, because it is a new tax and I realize that only by trial and error, as it were, can we establish a satisfactory basis in imposing new taxes. My purpose is rather to bring two or three points before the committee in order that we may consider what ought to be done to bring about that measure of equality of sacrifice about which we are hearing so much.
May I say in passing that several newspaper editorials have been commenting on what they allege to have been a statement of mine to the effect that something like twenty new millionaires had been created so far during the war. The house generally understood that I did not make that statement. I drew it to the attention of the minister because the statement had been made-I had heard it on more than one occasion-and I said at the time that I could find no figures to substantiate it.
When I look at several industries that were engaged in providing material for preparedness before the war broke out, it struck me last year, and it has struck me again this year, that these companies are in a more or less favoured position because their hasis was that of relatively high profits before the war broke out. Consequently they are able to obtain virtually the profits they had before the war and some little excess as well, whereas a company which was doing badly before the war is not in that position. I speak of the twenty-eight companies, and I shall be glad to
let the minister have my computation if he wishes to check my figures afterwards, when I have them a little more complete.
The Consolidated Mining and Smelting company ends its year on December 31. In 1939' they made profits of $9,340,000, in 1940 after paying all taxes, they made $9,062,000-a little1 less. As we go down the list we find that Aluminium Limited made a profit of $15,800,000 last year as against $12,462,000 the year before. I could cite a number of other companies whose profits after paying all taxes were almost the same, a little less or a little more than the year before. I am not forgetting that the year before was the first year which comprised part of the war period, when industrial expansion commenced. Some system of taxation should be devised to see that these companies contribute to our war effort to the full extent of their ability. We are appealing to people of quite small incomes to surrender what to them is a very large amount of purchasing power, considering what they had before, and many of us feel that during this period of war there must be a closer approach to equality of sacrifice than we have yet achieved. I know it will be argued that in addition to the taxes paid by these corporations, the people who receive the dividends will also pay a personal income tax. Nevertheless we should endeavour to find a basis which will take from the companies and corporations that are making large profits a greater proportion of their profits than we have yet taken. The government through its Department of Finance, after examining the statements that will be available within a short time, should be prepared to bring before the house when we meet again an excess profits tax that will bring from these companies larger contributions to the war effort than have so far been forthcoming.
In the war in which we are now engaged we shall have to think not in terms of money but in terms of goods and services. We have perhaps failed in the past to grasp the significant fact that we fight a war not with money but with goods and services, that the figures in the ledger are merely symbolic of our ability to do certain things. If we are to attain to a maximum war effort, instead of viewing our industrial effort in terms of profiits, dividends, financial resources and accumulated wealth, we must view it in the light of the nation's need for every conceivable thing that we can produce; for I am still of the opinion that Canada's maximum effort ought to be expended in the provision of the tools for which Mr. Churchill called a few months ago. I had hoped, therefore, that the returns from the thirty-three companies I discussed last

I did not make that

And may I add that I did it because I thought the Minister of Finance, or someone who knew something about these figures, might be able to suggest how such an impression arose outside the house.

Would
the hon. gentleman give the source from which these impressions come? I think the government ought to answer the indictment of these
{Mr. Coldwell.]
three big companies. I do not know anything about it. As to the matter of the twenty millionaires, I understand the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) has said that she has been told that there are forty new millionaires in Canada. Where did she get that information? This is part of the propaganda of the "have-nots" against the "haves," and it is based upon the imagination of someone who wants to do a disservice to Canada in war time.

I believe a statement should
be made by the minister, because I know of nothing more disquieting than these allegations about the creation of new millionaires. I believe every hon. member is against the idea of anyone making profit out of the war. In British Columbia the statement is heard that millionaires are being made every day; therefore a statement should be made by the minister.
Statements made out of whole cloth.

The hon. member for Red Deer asked for some information in that connection but his request was refused. A statement should be made in order to allay any unrest there may be throughout the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know how anyone can say how many millionaires there are in Canada, nor do I know how I could find out. The income tax returns, if gone over ever so carefully, would disclose only the amount of income. If that were broken down into investment income and earned income it might give some indication, but to do that would require an immense amount of research. I am morally certain and entirely satisfied that these statements, as to there being any particular number of millionaires in Canada, are wholly invented; that is, those making the statements have proceeded on nothing whatever. That remark does not apply to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar who, as he stated, did not make the assertion that there were some twenty odd new millionaires.
But he repeated the story.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He said he had heard it said, and he wanted to know if there was any information that could be given the house in that connection. Then the next day, if I remember correctly, he gave the basis for the statement, which I do not remember at the moment, but he admitted that it really was no basis at all.

Excess Profits Tax Act

The basis I was informed was the difference between the number of people getting more than $50,000 a year, as between the two years. In reply to someone who asked where the story began, the first time I heard the statement was during the Manitoba election, in and around the city of Winnipeg. I heard it there first; then I read it in one or two small newspapers. That really prompted my query in the house some days ago.

Under the present taxation set-up I do not see how millionaires could be created in Canada. The hon. gentleman says certain companies have made millions of dollars. That may be so, but if they paid that money out to their shareholders those shareholders would pay most of it back to the government in income tax. If money is in the treasury of a company it must stay there or be heavily taxed a second time, and the government has it fairly secure. It is true- and this may be a weakness in our present excess profits tax-that companies which were quite prosperous during a certain period before the war may be making a good deal of money at the present time and escape excess, because our excess profits tax is based on the principle that you shall not get rich out of the war. A company which was prosperous during the four-years computing period can still make a great deal of money for the company, but not for the shareholders, without again paying heavy personal income taxes. In my opinion, when you take 75 per cent of the profits of a company which was not any too prosperous before the war; then when you add to that 75 per cent all the other taxes that are being imposed, and take that money in cash, you may place a company in a hazardous position. Profits do not consist entirely of cash. In part they may consist of accounts receivable, which may become bad debts; they may consist in part of stock on hand, which may depreciate. The actual cash you take out of a company must not be too great a percentage of the profits or you will place the company in a difficult position.
Hon. gentlemen in the far corner are very critical in regard to taxes. To-day private industry is assuming a new role in Canada's economic system. When we have nationalized industry we have work carried on by the government; and I should like to ask the minister how much the government gets from these companies for the purpose of carrying on the affairs of the country, under this taxation law which is so important. If a private industry is able to quote the same figure as a government enterprise, which is
usually exempt from municipal, federal and many other taxes, I should say it would be very much more to the benefit of the government to do business with private industry, even at increased cost.
There is one other matter that I believe will be discussed more or less as time goes on; that is, what might be termed exemptions from taxation. The other day, when we were discussing the gasoline tax, I spoke against exemptions. I have been reading in the financial papers that in western Canada there are wheat pools that are making large profits each year, and I suppose those profits will become greater as the wheat remains stored in the elevators and does not circulate as freely as it did in other years. I believe the income tax law was changed in 1929 for the purpose of giving what might be called cooperatives a chance to get started, by exempting them from the payment of income tax. Well, cooperation is a splendid thing; I believe the establishment of and assistance to small cooperatives is in the interests of the country, but in connection with income tax we are dealing with excess, not only under the excess profits provision but in all instances. A man is allowed an exemption to an amount considered to be the minimum sufficient for him to get along, before his income is touched at all. A company must pay all its employees as an expense before it pays profits or any income tax, because such payments must be made before any profit can be shown. The expense of running an industry must be considered before you can compute the profit, so that when you deal with income tax in all its phases you are dealing with excess. Why should anyone in this country, especially in these critical days, escape the payment of a tax on any excess? The wheat pools, which operate under the shelter of cooperatives, do not pay income tax. I am told they have a financial and shareholders' structure that is rather mysterious, and they are becoming a commercial dictatorship in the west. Why should they, because of their power, be able to remain free from the payment of this tax when private industry is paying to such a large extent?
We are told that there is a new order; that there is a new way to do business; it is said that there is an easy way to get along, so that everybody will be satisfied. Well, I am all for that way if it is along the lines of cooperation; I am for every man having the greatest possible share of the fruits and profits of his labour. But every company should carry its own load, and I do not see why these pools in western Canada, which have piled up
Excess Profits Tax Act

millions of dollars in reserves, should be exempt from the payment of income tax. There is an easy way, I suggest, for them to get clear of any such tax; that is, by making their services to the farmers less expensive. Let the farmers receive the benefit of these cooperative methods; then the pools will have no income tax to pay.
I want to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance; and I want to say to him and his executive staff that private industry in this country, in its new role, has the government as its senior and probably its controlling partner. That may be good for private business; it may help do away with selfishness and greed on the part of men who we are told are becoming millionaires. It may be that these men who have been making a great deal of money, will now be working and making it for the state. And all men are not equal in ability or performance. Some men have superior qualities which others do not have. To-day they are being regimented to work for the state. It may be a good tfung. It may help the capitalistic system; it may clean the system. But at the same time every corporate company, everything which deals with limited liability enjoys some privileges, and should carry its share of the load of taxation. We are told there is a new order, one which is in competition with and which, it is said, will supplant the present competitive system. Let us see to it that there is a fair road and no favour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This does not impose any new burden on a corporation. It is an amelioration. As the act now stands-that is, the Excess Profits Tax Act passed in June, 1940-the constructive dividends received by corporate shareholders are taxable to the extent of the full rigours of the act, both at the 30 per cent rate and the 75 per cent rate. constructive dividends except in the exceptional cases of closely held companies referred to in the latter part of the section.

I asked the Minister of Finance the other day if he would give me an answer to a question which I posed at that time, with regard to the plateau of corporation profits in this country, using the years 1937 and 1929, compared with the experience in Great Britain where the base or standard profit period is 125 per cent of the 1929 plateau of profits, while in the United States it is probably about 66 or 67 per cent, using the 1937 earnings, as compared with the year 1929. In other words, it is of some consequence to industry and also, perhaps, of some consequence to our hon. friends on the left * to know just what base we use before we assess this excess profits tax.
I could never understand from a political angle why this government did not call this tax, not 75 per cent, but 79J per cent, which it certainly is if one makes the necessary calculations, because 79i per cent of every dollar of excess earnings above the somewhat low standard base, goes to the government, and in addition to that, in the two large indus' trial provinces, an additional 5 per cent is exacted for provincial revenues, making a total of 84^ per cent. That is quite substantial, and it is perhaps higher than now obtains in the old country, whose practices our hon. friends of the left are always citing, because there is now a 20 per cent drawback there in the form of a certificate to be used for corporate purposes after the war. If the minister has any figures, or if he con. siders that the proposal which I have suggested .regarding the levels of the corporate profits , in the respective countries is out of line with practical experience, I shall be very glad if he will let me know.
, Mr. ILSLEY: I have not any figures, and I do not see the significance of the comparison with 1929. The comparison with 1929 has quite a different meaning, I should think, in England, from the comparison with 1929 in ; the United States. I have not made a study of this, but I should think the level of earnings in the United States in 1929 was much higher than it was in Great Britain. I do not 1 believe there was any such boom in Great Britain as there was in the United States. Why is this year, 1929, being used as a base for comparison? The year we took is not 1929; we adopted the four years 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939, whether they were high or low compared with 1929.
IMr. Douglas G. Ross.]

I used the year 1929 because it was looked upon as an extremely profitable one practically throughout the world; for, as we know, good times are more or less universal. It is true, I think, to say that the level of prosperity because of control of inflation in Great Britain was not as high as in the United States, nevertheless it was a prosperous time. I should be willing to use the period 1926-29 or any other, and if I am asked why 1929 was singled out, I simply answer that it was customary to take that year. We find that when the Department of Labour fixed their index or freezing point for wage scales they used the period 1926-29, or any period since then, and allowed the highest wage obtaining during any part of that time as the level which labour might obtain before applying for an increase in consequence of the rise in the cost of living. In my opinion, the year 1929 in industry is not an unfair one, but I should be glad if the Department of Finance would use any other so that we might know whether or not the taking away of 841 per cent by the dominion and provincial authorities is a taking away after a fair allowance is made to the corporation.
I realize, of course, that there are other purposes behind the excess profits tax besides the taking of money out of the hands of shareholders, one object being to prevent inflation; and while it may not be entirely germane to the subject at the moment, it would be interesting to know-and I do not think it is entirely theoretical-whether or not the minister or his department looks upon the excess profits tax as anti-inflationary or definitely inflationary. There is unquestionably, on the one hand, a taking away of excess profits or additional earnings from shareholders so that they cannot spend them and thus tend to increase the prices of goods generally; and on the other hand-I know this view is held by some economists-it is considered that the management of corporations, knowing that an increase in wages, or an addition, or some expensive maintenance will in effect be borne to the extent of 84J per cent by the government, are not as prone to be as careful as if they themselves had a larger stake in the expenditures under consideration. Therefore we have the possibility of this very measure, which may have been designed as an antiinflation measure as well as one for the purpose of producing revenue, becoming something of a boomerang.
I realize, however, that that is a question to which some consideration will have to be given, and I shall not press for an answer

Excess Profits Tax Act
now. I suggest that these matters should come before the house from time to time so that hon. members might appreciate their significance. I cannot help recalling that when the excess profits tax first came up it seemed to every member of the house, or at any rate to 95 per cent of the membership, that it was designed solely for the purpose of preventing any war profiteering; and with that in view it received the unanimous approval of the house. In fact, certain members proposed a higher tax. But there was another reason behind it, namely, to put us under a controlled economy and to do away with the profit motive in the production of goods, which was an entirely different matter. I cannot help feeling that the minister has not taken the house into his confidence, and, if I may go so far as to say so, he has not used the utmost good faith in presenting the measure to the house, not letting us know exactly what the implications were; because it is a major step to pass from a free economy, where the profit motive prevails, to one where there is a controlled economy, everything being under the government and the instinct to better one's position is not the motivating one.

I suggest that they are being unduly penalized. I suggest that the minister is not giving consideration to the success of small businesses, nor is he taking due regard of the importance of managerial ability.
I have many protests in my portfolio respecting this matter. I would urge the minister to give favourable consideration to the limitations he has suggested respecting small businesses. The capital invested may be only a small amount. That is the base upon which the action is taken. It is not sufficiently wide in the case of small businesses, and a real injustice is being done to some people in Canada. If the base could be widened it might take away some of their difficulties. There has been a great deal of competition, and I make my appeal on their behalf.

I would associate

With my meagre experience I would judge that all these regulations are of a nature such as to make it almost impossible for the small business to establish itself and to continue operations.

I do not wish to labour the point, because I know the minister and his officials are conversant with it, but it is not often an hon. member rises and places before the government opportunities to bring in more revenue. That, in effect, is my proposal under section 10 of the bill. By the amendment moved last week, investment companies with senior capital were removed from this exemption from excess profits tax. I believe I should point out to the committee that investment companies are free, practically without restraint, to hold in their portfolios those forms of securities which they deem best. If they hold the stocks of other Canadian companies, a tax having already been paid by those corporations, the stock on which the dividend is paid is free in the hands of the investment companies.
With bond interest it is otherwise, because the debtor company has not paid a tax on it, and the interest, when it comes to the investment company, must be subjected to taxation. It works out, however, that in the management of these companies it is impossible to live with a 40 per cent tax-which is the minimum, if the excess profits tax applies-applied to income merely because it stops at a station along the line, before reaching the ultimate beneficiary. That particular station does nothing; it acts merely as a trustee in the collection and disbursing of the money.
Therefore, if the minister is interested in collecting revenue he will endeavour, if it is at all possible, to make an exemption of this
Excess Profits Tax Act

class of company having senior capital. He will find then that he will get more tax, because they will hold more bonds on which they will pay the 18 per cent, or the normal corporation tax to the treasury. He will get more in that way than he will receive if he simply applies the excess profits tax of 40 per cent, which they cannot stand. They would have to turn round, take their funds out of the bonds, and put them into preferred or common stock.
I believe the minister will see the force of the argument when he realizes that there are many good preferred stocks on the market which to all intents and purposes have the qualities of bonds, sell at comparable levels and bring in comparable yields. Therefore, while I know it may seem odd for a member to rise in his place to do as I am doing, yet I am in a sense endeavouring to make matters harder for the taxpayer. I do that because they simply cannot continue paying 40 per cent, but of necessity and by reason of the government's action would have to place their funds in securities which are not taxable. On the other hand, if they are permitted to pay the 18 per cent tax, they will feel that that is still a burden under which they can operate.
I feel quite confident when I say that the minister will receive more revenue if he does as I suggest than if he permits the measure to pass in its present form.
One other point. The limit of time before which 85 per cent of the net income for the year must be distributed is ninety days. Perhaps this is not a very important point, but may I add that when you distribute 85 per cent of the income of a company you do not leave much margin to go on. For instance, at the present time a company the fiscal year of which ends with the calendar year will find itself being audited, and the exact taxation may not be known. Therefore it is in a position perhaps of declaring a dividend which may leave insufficient available. If it makes no difference to the department I would suggest a period of one hundred and twenty days, which is the same length of time within which the taxes are returned, and after which a penalty must be paid.
I would also point out that there has to be an extra amount of time, on account of the provision of the foreign exchange control board respecting thirty days' notice after declaration of dividends. Therefore a period of one hundred and twenty days would not be unreasonable, and would simplify operations.

I think the corporation tax is altogether inequitable, especially as applied to small incomes. As soon as it was announced in the budget that there was to be an increase of 10 per cent, capital values decreased. I suggest that it would be better to maintain capital values. When there is a decline in capital values, the effect is felt by such concerns as insurance companies. I am not suggesting that the tax should not be collected; I merely urge that it be collected after a person gets his income and not before.
Take the Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto. That company has had a hard time getting along all these years.
