One matter I wish to draw to the attention of the minister has to do with the spawning beds on the Fraser river and its tributaries. In 1913 and before we had the catastrophe at Hell's Gate that blocked the salmon from getting up the Fraser river to spawn, there was in British Columbia a total pack of about 2,500,000 cases of what is known as the Fraser river salmon. That includes the salmon packed on the United States side as well as on the Canadian side but it all goes under the Fraser river system catch. The value of that pack was approximately $30,000,000.
Then we had the rock slide, and since that time and with the intensive fishing that has taken place, the runs have gone down each year. If we take the good years-and I quote 1934 as one of the good years for sockeye-the total pack of sockeye salmon in that year was about half a million cases of a value of about $7,000,000.
To bring the matter more vividly to the attention of the committee, let me say that in 1913 British Columbia packed 684,596 cases of sockeye salmon. This pack from fish caught
in the Fraser river was more than the entire United States and Canadian pack from the Fraser river system in 1940.
What I particularly wish to bring to the minister's attention is the fact that large power corporations in British Columbia have been allowed to build dams on certain tributary streams of the Fraser river, and that these dams have in some measure contributed to the depletion of our fisheries in the Fraser river system. Four dams in all have been built on tributaries of the Fraser. The first was built in 1898 on the outlet from Coquitlam lake in order to provide water for the city of Vancouver. The attention of the authorities of Vancouver was drawn at that time to the fact that this might interfere with salmon going up to spawn, and the authorities were requested to put in a fishway, to enable the salmon to get over the dam and so on to the spawning beds. Later improvements were made at this particular lake, but the dam was later built higher and so the fish-ladder was not made adequate and was pronounced a failure.
As I pointed out, there are, in all, four dams. But the one that I particularly wish to bring to the minister's attention is the Alouette dam built by the Burrard Power Company, a subsidiary of the British Columbia Electric. The Alouette dam is located in the south fork of the Alouette river at the mouth of Alouette lake. The construction began in 1924 and was completed early in 1927. It raised the level of the lake by about seventy feet and diverted the waters through a tunnel to Stave lake where the power-house was located. The plan operates under an authorized head of 125 feet and is automatically controlled from the Stave falls generating station. At the present time there is often little or no water flowing in the south channel of the Alouette river. In fact, for many months in the year the bed of that river is absolutely dry. Before the construction of the dam, all five species of salmon, and steelheads, entered this lake. For example, on October 16, 1923, Inspector A. P. Halliday visited Alouette river and lake and found chum and pink salmon very numerous. He also counted eight sockeye and four spring salmon in the south Alouette river within a period of forty minutes.
Following the erection of the dam, sockeye were observed by officers of the Department of Fisheries and of the biological board of Canada, one of whom was Doctor Foerster, later of the salmon commission staff. In 1927 the lake apparently was first blocked to the ascent of salmon. On July 3, 1929, the south Alouette was nearly dry when about two thousand sockeye were noted below the first
Supply-Fish eries

falls in the north fork of the Alouette river. An attempt was made to transfer these fish above the falls by dip net, but those so transferred only fell back over the falls again. On July 6 the run had entirely disappeared from both the north and south forks of the river. In 1930 several thousand were seen in the north Alouette toward the end of May, and a little later many thousand tried to ascend the dam in the south Alouette, there having been a good overflow at that time. This was the last run of early sockeye salmon observed since this dam and the Coquitlam dam have cut off their spawning grounds. The dam after completion wras impassable to salmon, and no fishway was provided. It is not certain just why a fishway was not placed over the dam, but apparently it was believed that this was not feasible, and that the power from this project was more valuable than the Alouette fisheries.
I bring up this matter because I believe that before long the building of dams will reach serious proportions and greatly affect the salmon industry; for it should be pointed out that the Fraser river, with its tributaries, has been mapped for power purposes by engineers of the provincial government. Many companies, I believe, are seeking power sites there, and I have no doubt that before very long they will be asking for the right to construct dams across the Fraser as well as its tributaries. Here we have an instance of four dams having been built on streams up which sockeye and other salmon went to spawn. These salmon now have disappeared because they could not get over the dams.
At the time attention was drawn to this situation, and the statement was made that a fishway was not feasible. The great work that has since been carried on in the United States had not been commenced. I have in my hand to-night, however, a copy of the booklet put out by the government of the United States with regard to what took place with reference to the Bonneville dam on the Columbia river near Portland. There the authorities compelled the builders of the dam to put in a fishway so that salmon might ascend the river to spawn. In addition, I understand, they had to spend a considerable amount of money to provide a means of bringing the young fry down again, because they discovered that when the young fingerlings were allowed to come over the waterfall many of them were killed. I am told that the total cost of providing the fishway, and the method of bringing the fingerlings down again, was in the neighbourhood of 815,000,000. In any event the fishery officers of the state of Washington maintain that these fishways or fish-ladders are a success. At the Bonneville dam they 
raise the fish a height of two hundred feet, to the level of the lake system above, and there is a flume or pipe for bringing back the fingerlings. In British Columbia, however, we allowed the large power corporations to go ahead and construct dams on our rivers without protest.
At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I pointed out the great value of that fishery in 1930 compared with the value to-day, and in order to emphasize my point I am going to repeat those figures. In 1913 there was packed something like 830,000,000 worth of canned salmon, whereas last year the total pack was valued at not more than 87,000,000. If this situation is allowed to continue, that fishery will become non-existent. At the moment I am not going to deal with the work of the international fisheries commission, of which I am a member, but this is the proper place to bring up the question of these dam obstructions. A number of years ago the Fisheries Act was amended to give the minister authority to compel companies or corporations placing obstructions on these rivers to provide fishways or dams to permit the salmon to ascend. That authority is contained in section 20 of the act. I am not going to read the whole section, but I should like to read subsection 7;
The minister may require the owner or occupier of any slide, dam or other obstruction to instal and maintain such fish stops or diverters, both above and below any dam or obstruction as will in his opinion be adequate to prevent the destruction of fish and/or to assist in providing for their ascent.
My appeal to the minister this evening is that he take steps to compel this company, if necessary, even at this late date to put in fishways in order that salmon may reach the upper streams and lakes to spawn. I know someone will say that this company was given the right to do these things in days gone by, and that it would be hardly fair to make it put in these fishways now. My reply would be that the power contained in this act was inserted for this very purpose, and I know there have been occasions in this country when action of this kind was taken after appeals had been made to the minister. I am not going to weary the committee at greater length in this connection, but I thought, . this was the proper time to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and to ask him to give my appeal every consideration.

What the hon. member for New Westminster has said with respect to obstructions across salmon rivers will find its counterpart in the history of every salmon stream on the Atlantic coast west of New Brunswick. There was a time

Supply-Fisheries
when every river in New England was a salmon fishing river. There was a time when Penobscot salmon held the same place in the markets of New England that Gaspe salmon holds to-day in Canada. That is all a thing of the past now because of the construction of dams for power purposes without proper provision for the preservation of the salmon fisheries. Surely we have learned something in a quarter or a third of a century; and I am certain that our department, so far as it has jurisdiction, will not be unmindful of the lessons of the past.
I know nothing of the situation to which the hon. member has referred, but I have no reason to doubt that he has correctly stated it. Efforts have been made from time to time on the Atlantic coast to authorize the construction of dams on some of our salmon rivers. Such efforts have been valiantly opposed except when adequate provision was made for the propagation of this species of fish. I hope the minister will give heed to what the hon. gentleman has said. Great progress has been made in the scientific construction of fish-ladders. Years ago I was very much interested in this sort of thing; and if my information is correct, I am quite satisfied that there are now in service fish-ladders which will perform a useful function. They may not be one hundred per cent perfect, but they will go a long way toward meeting the situation.

After the minister deals with salmon runs and dams on the different rivers, perhaps he might give the committee some information with regard to lobster control, about which there is a good deal of comment in the newspapers and on which a large amount of money has been spent. I understand that in the supplementary estimates $600,000 was provided for this purpose, of which $158,000 was spent.

The statements made
by the hon. member for New Westminster, and supported by the leader of the opposition are certainly of great interest and importance at the present time. In years gone by, facilities to aid the fish to get over dams had not been fully developed. We know that today some experiments have been made, and have been successful. That is particularly true in recent years in the United States. But the authority to permit the building of dams across streams in non-tidal waters is one which rests with provincial governments.

What
about international rivers?

I believe the provinces have claimed autonomy and jurisdiction with respect to rivers without tidal waters and
within provincial limits. I believe the international joint commission controls the volume of water running in such rivers. The provinces, however, have always claimed jurisdiction over permits for the erection of structures or obstructions in non-tidal waters within their limits.

On the
theory that they own the bed of the stream, to the centre?
Yes.
And what about an international river, such as the St. Croix? For instance, who authorized the dam at Woodlands?
That was erected before my time.
That is so.

The only control the
dominion government through the Department of Fisheries has maintained over these obstructions in rivers has been the right of insisting that proper facilities be provided to permit of the descent and ascent of fish. This is provided by the Fisheries Act, as amended in 1939.
Those who have given any study to the great industry of fishing know that the Fraser river is the most important of our salmon rivers in Canada. It holds that position because of the large number of fish travelling those waters, and resorting to them for purposes of propagation. The high value of the type of fish caught in that river gives added importance to it. It must be understood that in the main Fraser river there are no artificial obstructions or dams. Some years ago, however, three large dams were built on three streams in the Fraser river system. As the hon. member for New Westminster has said, the first dam, built on the Coquitlam river, was built in 1898. and was so built for the purpose of providing a storage of water for human consumption by the residents of Vancouver. A situation was faced whereby it became necessary to provide water for the large population of that city, and it was considered that the point I have mentioned offered the only possible storage facilities available. It was decided at that time that it was more important to provide water for the citizens of Vancouver and district than to leave the river open so that the fish might ascend it. It was considered that there were many other streams in the system which could be developed for fisheries purposes. In this instance the dam was built to a height of 100 feet.

That
could not be blamed on the power companies.
Supply-Fisheries

No, not that one. Then, a dam 130 feet high was built some years ago for power purposes on a stream or creek known as the Stave river. In 1934 another dam, 125 feet high, was built farther down the same stream. It was thought absolutely necessary at the time to provide storage for power purposes, and inasmuch as other streams or rivers were available to the fish, it was thought this one might very well be sacrificed. It was considered impracticable at the time to provide satisfactory fishways or ladders in that river.
Then, in 1927 the dam was built in the Alouette river. The records show that there was a great demand for power in that district from the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster. At that time public authorities, both provincial and federal, thought they might very well overlook the fishing interests and develop more power on that stream. Accordingly they erected a high dam, in which it was impossible to build a fishway. This dam raised by forty or fifty feet the water level above the dam, and it is impossible for the fish to spawn in that depth of water. Then, below stream, during most of the summer season the stream is dry, because the water is stored purposely to provide for emergencies. Therefore, even if a proper fish-ladder or fishway had been built in that dam, it would have been of no avail, because it would not have permitted spawning.
It could not have operated successfully.

No; it could not have operated successfully. Those are the only three streams on the whole Fraser river system which have been dammed, and in which fishways have not been provided. Since that time, to my knowledge there has been no demand for more power which would bring further impediment to fishing on the streams of the Fraser river. If there were such demands I am sure the provincial authorities would consider the matter seriously before granting authorization to build dams. The Department of Fisheries would take every precaution to see that proper facilities were constructed, by way of fish-ladders or other devices, to permit of the ascent of the fish. Therefore I can assure the hon. member for New Westminster that when the occasion arises he may rest assured that the provincial and federal authorities will try to preserve the great asset of the Fraser river, because they realize that sockeye fishing is the backbone of the industry on the Pacific coast.

It is passing strange that when the first dam was built and built for water purposes for a city, the fisheries authorities

demanded of the city that a fishway be constructed for the fish; and yet when the power corporations come along and build their dam, no demand is made by the fisheries department that a fishway be placed on the dam so that the fish can go up. It is true, as the minister said, that one dam caused a great depth of water which prohibits the sockeye and other salmon from spawning. But the Fisheries Act contains a provision compelling the companies to build not only fishways but hatcheries. Hatcheries should have been built there at the expense of the company to look after the young fingerlings. These power companies, however, as was pointed out by the leader of the opposition, have gone ahead in a ruthless manner, their only thought being to develop power projects, with no thought of what disaster might take place in the fisheries when the dams are built.
One other thought I leave with the minister. It is true that at that time the fisheries authorities did not consider a fishway was feasible, but since then the United States has experimented with dams, as in the Bonny-ville dam where the fish are taken over a height of over 200 feet without injury at all. This is claimed to be a success, and in the light of that experience I think the minister should ask these companies for a statement of their intentions now. I do not think it is right to allow them to escape the responsibility which was certainly theirs two years ago. The damage can be proven. The minister should at least have an inquiry into the possible damage if my presentation strikes him as in any respect doubtful.

On the question 6f jurisdiction, it is quite clear that the federal authority has some jurisdiction. Even so it, cannot prohibit the erection of a dam in a non-tidal water. My understanding is, however, that the federal authority has jurisdiction with respect to the regulation of the flow of water for the preservation of the fisheries, which of course are under dominion jurisdiction. Therefore no one can with impunity build a dam without taking into account the rights of the dominion, even though the province should give authority. What is the policy of the department? Have they watched these applications carefully, and what happened?

That has been the policy of the department for the last forty years, so far as I have been able to learn. The hon. member for New Westminster stated that when the dam was built on the Coquitlam stream the dominion government insisted that there

Supply-Fisheries
should be a passageway for the fish, but afterwards it did not insist when the power companies built their dams. I cannot answer for what was done forty years ago. After the first dam was built, it was found that instead of being useful it was a great detriment, not so much to the fish, as to the users of the water, the residents of Vancouver. It was found that quite a number of fish died in that basin, and the health authorities claimed that the use of the water was dangerous to the * health of the citizens of Vancouver.
Did they abandon the river?

No; the fishway was abandoned.
As to the attitude of the Department of Fisheries, some years later when the other dams were built it was found that it was not practicable to insist on having fishways as they were then built, with dams a hundred feet high, because the automatic ladder was not then in use, I am informed, and accordingly the department did not insist on having fishways put in the dams. These are the reasons I find on record.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to think that among some of my friends at least there seems to be an idea that the introduction of these estimates is an annual opportunity for me to attack the department and all connected with it.	I assure the
committee that that is far from being my desire or my interest. My sole object is to preserve the fishing industry in British Columbia and to protect the interests of those concerned in it-the canners on the one hand, more or less in a position of antagonism, and the fishermen on the other. I think the day will come when they will realize that their interests can be brought together instead of suggesting that whatever the one class wants, the other must oppose. I do not need to protest often on behalf of the interests of the canners because the telescope through which British Columbia fishing matters are eyed from Ottawa contains an official lens manufactured in Vancouver through which the interests of the cannery men are reflected in such a favourable light that there is never any danger of their interests not being very much to the fore and very well looked after.
In connection with the general estimates of the fisheries department, considering this is war time-if it were not war time I would be asking for a lot more money to be spent- I do not think there is much to be found fault with in these estimates. Departmental
administration-that means the office holders -is down a little. The amount appropriated for fishery inspection, including fishery officers and guardians, and control is left as it was. It should have been increased. There is an increase for building fishways and clearing rivers. That is to the good. Therp is a reduction in the estimates for saltfish boards and so forth-all to the good.
There is one increase for which I commend the minister, namely, for obtaining a grant for a fishery bounty for the destruction of hair-seals. The bounty was stopped last year or two years ago, and a more false economy could not have been thought of, because, when you have spent money over a series of years to put down a pest like that, there is no more fatal thing than to give them an open period again. That was done in British Columbia with wolves. When they had sot the wolves down to a minimum, and a more liberal amount spent on the remaining wolves would have cleared them off for all time, a foolish economy stopped the bounty altogether and gave the remaining wolves a nice period in which they were practically preserved, thus giving them a new lease of life. The consequence was that the wolves increased in numbers and another bounty had to be offered. The minister has done well in these times, when money is so short, to put this bounty on again. It will be appreciated by the fishermen and by all branches of the industry.
There are just two items which I wish particularly to mention. My custom in the past was not to bring these matters up on the floor of the house unless I failed to get reasonable attention through the usual official channels. I mention these two items to-night not in any spirit of attack on the minister.
One is with regard to the pack. I am afraid that some mistake or misunderstanding has occurred which certainly needs to be cleared up, and cleared up speedily. There was the usual dispute last year between the cannery men and the fishermen about price. Hon. members can understand that the war deprived us of a great deal of the British market.
The British government had indicated that they were not going to buy the high class salmon, that is the sockeye; they were going to buy the cheapest grade, which had the same food value as had the higher-priced salmon. That, of course, cut the market from below the fishermen for their valuable and expensive fish, the sockeye, and there was a great deal of dispute about the matter. I suggested to the ministry that they should try to establish a policy or make an arrangement
Supply-Fisheries

between the two bodies, that the price of the fish should be at a certain standard, with the understanding that if the price went up in the fall the fishermen should get a part of the increased profit. But that was not attended to, and the result was that the fishermen had to go and fish at what was then, apparently, a very low price, because the canners said, and with justice, "We do not know whether we shall be able to sell the higher-priced fish at any reasonable price, and therefore we would be taking an enormous loss if we paid the usual higher price for the better fish."
I foresaw the possibility of what would happen. The fishermen had to go to work for this lower price; they were told it was their duty, that there was a war on, and that they would not get any more. But the price did go up, as I anticipated. The British or some other market developed, and the canneries made quite a killing, because they had made a bargain covering the whole year. Feeling became so intense, however, that they themselves agreed to a considerable increase towards the end of the season. This incident caused great dissatisfaction among the fishermen, who thought they had been gypped. I did not wish to see that happen again. Accordingly, last fall I wrote to the minister and suggested that he send, or take advantage of one of his officials going, to London and see if he could not arrange ahead with the British government to take what they required at a fixed price, and then they would be in a position to negotiate with prospects of a better price to the fishermen, because if the canners could dispose of the whole of their pack they would be relieved of brokerage and other costs of selling. That was not done; and now I go into the realm of imagination, because I do not know what took place. But some communication passed between the British government and this government early this spring. Judging by the newspapers-for that is the only method by which I can find out anything-the deputy minister went out to British Columbia, and it was reported in the newspapers that he went with the purpose of making arrangements with the British government to take the whole pack. Here are some headings in the Vancouver papers:
Ottawa to take over whole B.C. pack, is rumour.
Deputy fisheries minister interviews trade in Vancouver. Explains trip.
Proposed acquisition of the entire British Columbia salmon pack by the Canadian government to ensure food fish supplies for Canada's armed forces, while stabilizing exports to the United Kingdom, is reported to be the major reason for the present visit to Vancouver of Doctor D. B. Finn, Deputy Minister of Fisheries.

Another paper said that he was there for the purpose of-
-getting sufficient information in the matter of commandeering the salmon pack.
What time of the year would that be?

That would be April 24-
quite recently. The next thing we heard was that the deal had fallen through. I asked a question in the house, and the minister told me very much to the same effect, conveyed of course in rather vague language, that his deputy had been out with a view of looking into the subject and getting a basis for the purchase of the pack by the British government. Be it right or be it wrong, it is not my mistake; at any rate, that was the general impression created among the public out there. Later on we were advised that there was nothing to it; that the fish were going to be bought in the ordinary way by the British government if and when they wanted them, and at any price that they could arrange; in fact, it was all left up in the air.
This has made matters very awkward for the fishermen. They will have to go out and fish: a fisherman has to go out when the fish are running. The only chance of successfully conducting negotiations is by starting beforehand. Down the years we have begun to get a little better feeling between the canners, who had their organization, and the fishermen, who had various unions. They had begun to realize that getting together was the proper thing to do. Now they are all up in the air; the fishermen are sore, the canners are sore, and they do not know what it is all about. I see in the press evidences of dissatisfaction from their point of view; nobody knows where he is getting off at. The minister, I have no doubt, will explain; but what I would much rather have is some definite action in the future. There is no doubt that the British government should announce, as they appear willing to do, that they are buying a certain quantity. When they have stated what they require, and roughly how much they are willing to pay

or even without that information-we could go to the canners and to the fishermen and say, "Now, get together. You fishermen have a sure market for what you catch, and you canners have an assured market for what you can, and under these conditions you can both afford to take a lower price than before." Or. rather, the fishermen cannot afford to go lower than last year, because not only has the cost of living advanced, but the cost of gear has gone up very much. That is something about which I should like to see the minister give us an explanation.

Supply-Fisheries
While I am on my feet I might as well deal with another matter. It is one with which the present minister and myself are familiar over long years; it is one with which previous ministers and deputy ministers who were in power in the years gone by were very familiar.

Old
friends, in other words.

Old enemies-I do not mean
the deputies, but the question. What I have been agitating for many years is that the government should not allow herrings to be reduced. When you reduce a fish you turn it into meal and oil; you extract the oil from it, and then you turn the rest of it, bone and everything else, into meal which can be used for fertilizer, or, in other words, for manure for the land, or for feeding stock and so forth. I might explain that it would not pay to reduce herrings by themselves, because the amount of oil you get out of the herring is comparatively small. It is possible to do this only at the end of the reduction season for pilchards. The pilchard is a fish which comes from heaven knows where. It does not spawn in our waters, and therefore we cannot take too many of them. They are full of oil; they give two to three times as much as a herring would. I do not think it would pay to build and run a reduction plant for herrings alone; but when the fishing season for pilchards is over, and herrings come at the end of it, it is feasible for the plant owners to operate for two or three months and make something more than their expenses, so keeping down their overhead. The point is that when you are using pilchards for reduction you are using fish which can be utilized for very little else. Attempts have been made to can them, but the market is small, and it does not seem to be increasing. It would be practicable, I suppose, to sell them only in south American or Italian countries, where they call for very cheap and oily fish. At any rate they have been put up, but not very successfully; it is more profitable to use them for reduction purposes.
Herring, however, is a different matter altogether. The supply of pilchards is unlimited; if they happen to come your way they are so numerous that they are almost on your doorstep; if they do not, they are further out at sea, and whatever we do has no influence on them. But with the herrings it is different. They are a fish which should be used for human food. To use them for anything else is a crime and a shame, and that is being demonstrated now, when we need cheap food for our army and for the British army, and cannot get what we want, because they have been fished out to make manure
and cow food in days gone by. It has been said, "Herrings are unlimited; you find them all over the Pacific ocean; you cannot fish them out." But it is not so. Where you catch herrings is in the inlets, and places like that, where they come to spawn. I have seen, in an area not much bigger than from here to Wellington street, thirty huge seine boats, and so close that they could not all fish at once. They had to take turns, and when one boat pulled out with 30,000 fish, another came in. It was just one continuous drain on the fish as they came in to spawn. Herrings, however, are peculiar that way; you cannot fish them out, but you can harass them so that they will go away, and they will go away for twenty years.
I can name harbours, Nanaimo for one, and there are two or three in my own riding, where they quit, and it was from fifteen to twenty years before they came back.
Every fisherman will tell you, because it is a proverb, "No herring, no salmon." The reason is that the herring is the food of the salmon. There are scientific experts who would like to make it appear that the herring is not the food of the salmon; therefore they go to some place where herrings do not run, catch a salmon, open it, and examine the contents of its stomach, and when they find no herring in the stomach they profess to prove that herring is not the food of the salmon. Well, of course, they do not find any herring in the stomachs of salmon in that particular place. On one occasion, I believe, they found a piece of rubber tire in the stomach of a salmon. One wonders whether they would suggest that the salmon fed on rubber tires. The fact is that the herring is the main food of the salmon, in addition to a small plant known as lance.
The reduction of herring results in the diminution of salmon. It is not so much a matter of taking the herrings for canning alone; they could stand that. But when you superimpose on top of that the extra drain for reduction purposes, then the drain is too much and they go away. I recall an occasion -I think it is time for plain speaking-when it did not suit the officials in the past to agree with me on this question. Those officials are [DOT] not here to-day, and therefore it does not matter my mentioning this. They did not agree with me that the herring run on the west coast of Vancouver island was getting smaller, and consequently I produced a report submitted by the officials of their own biological board. Thej are known by another name to-day; there is, I believe, a fancy name for them now. At any rate, they said
Supply-Fisheries

that the run was getting smaller, and they demonstrated by scientific means the extent to which it was decreasing. One of these men got a tip from Ottawa not to make such a report again because a report of that sort was not acceptable at Ottawa, for the simple reason that Ottawa did not believe, and in fact did not wish to believe, that the herring run was being depleted. But it was being depleted.
I have always contended that herring reduction alone was not profitable. You barely-get by under the conditions that I have indicated. The pilchard industry is the one in which you make money. There is a danger of the herring being completely eliminated, with the prospect of its ceasing to be the food of the salmon, and the salmon will stop going there. I can point to areas where you cannot catch a single fish now but where fish used to be caught.
The other day I wrote a letter to the minister-on May 9, to be exact-enclosing a copy of a letter I had received from a fisherman who, I said in my letter, I knew was a reputable man representing reputable peoplej In that letter I pointed out to the minister what this man had said, and I will summarize this fisherman's contention. He said that he had gone into a place and was cod fishing with a friend at a time of the year when it was necessary to get codfish because there was nothing else to live on. He had1 gone into this area to get herring bait for codfish and there were no herrings. There were boats there trying to catch fish for bait, but there were no herrings. He goes into details. He says that there were from eighty to ninety boats waiting for herring to come but none appeared, and he himself stayed there for several days. He complains that the seining of the herring for reduction has resulted in the clean up.
According to figures that had been given, the seine boats took out 4,722 tons. The fishermen say that if these herrings were used for domestic or canning purposes it would be all right, but they are used for fertilizer, a thing that should be stopped. The minister or his officials, in correspondence coming from the department, will suggest, "Oh, these things are not so; it is an exaggeration. The catch of herrings on the Pacific coast is increasing." Yes, it is increasing; why ? Because they are going further and further north. A quota was put on at one time. The local minister said that he would put on a quota that would forever settle the question, because he would allow only a reasonable amount of herrings to be used for reduction purposes. I wrote back and said, "You need not put on a quota because you 
will raise it every time the canners want you to". And that very season he raised it, because the local government has power, in connection with the regulation of canning' to raise the quota. The canner always gets the quota increased if he so desires. I have seen it increased, sometimes twice a year. When, therefore, it is said that the catch is increasing, I reply that the reason is .that the herring fishers are going further and further north. The fishermen went up north and discovered herrings which they had not suspected were there. No quota was put on them because it was not known what a fair quota would be, and unlimited herrings were taken before a quota could be put on.
I have been following up this correspondence for years and years. It has been alleged that there was a dispute between the provincial and dominion governments, and it was not known whether we had the power. The point was raised that section 29 of the Fisheries Act was rather ambiguously worded, and it was not clear whether the dominion government had any control over fish after it was caught. The idea was that we had control over the catching and taking of the fish and could prohibit this, but that once it was caught and in the hands of the fisherman he could do whatever he liked with the fish. The local government had the power of licensing reduction plants, and they could take such action in this regard as they wished.
With a fresh outburst of hopefulness, which experience did not at all justify, I took the matter up again last September, and the department and I have been pleasantly exchanging correspondence since. It was argued that the matter was not settled. It was taken up with the Department of Justice and a definite ruling has been given, which I presume will have to be accepted unless it is contested in the courts. We cannot control the fish after it is dead, after it is caught, but we can say that no fish shall be caught for reduction purposes. We can say to those who take these fish for canning purposes, "If your intention is to reduce the fish you shall not be allowed to catch it." That is all the power we need. The provincial government could stop them by refusing a licence, but they do not. But the dominion government can and,
I urge, should say, "We will not allow you to take herrings if it is your intention to reduce them. It is argued, however, that when you can herrings there is a lot of the fish-the offal, the guts, and head and tail-which is of no value. A certain quantity of fish is brought in in huge scows, 500 tons; some will be crushed so that they are unsuitable for canning; or they get stale. There will be a

Supply-Fisheries
certain proportion that should go to the reduction plant, and for that reason, argued the department, it is necessary to allow these people to reduce all the herrings they like. But does not common sense suggest that it is and should be possible to allow them to can all the herrings they like and also to allow them to reduce the offal, or crushed or damaged fish? There could be an inspection of the scow to determine whether they should be allowed to reduce the fish, but these people should not be given the privilege of imposing a double drain on the fishing resources of the country by carrying on both reducing and canning at the same time.
In the last two years, since the war began, there has been a huge increase in the demand for canned herring. Too much of it cannot be got, and now is the time to take the necessary action in this matter. There is no reason why some provision should not be made so that while they could catch herring only for canning purposes, yet such portions as were not in a condition to be canned might be reduced. The department, something like Hitler-no, it is the Russians-have a five-year plan. Whenever you try to get the fisheries department to say or do something definite they always bring out of their hip-pocket a plan by which they are going to investigate for five years or eight years, and if you do not die in the meantime, they will look into it at the end of that time. But I am getting to be an old man; I would like some action; I have been at this for fifteen years pressing the government, and there is not a fisherman in British Columbia who is not of the same opinion. Even the canners are now seeing it. I would go on my knees to induce the minister, and would never worry him any more if he would stop the reduction of herring.

As usual the presentation of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is interesting. His long experience of the fishing industry on the Pacific coast makes his observations always helpful, and he always makes very good suggestions.
As to the matters upon which he desires information, first, his suggestion that the department should send someone to London to try to dispose of or find ways of increasing the sale of salmon packed in British Columbia, I may say that the facilities of the Canadian government and the department were offered to the British government within a month after the declaration of war. Since then, every opportunity has been taken to keep in close touch with British requirements, and communications through the usual channels have been going on regularly with a view to keeping Britain supplied with as much as possible of the products of the Canadian fishing
industry. Last winter we found that last year's pack of canned salmon was already disposed of. There was no difficulty whatever in disposing of last year's pack both on the home market and on the other usual markets, Australia, New Zealand, south Africa-
Was that through the usual channels?

Yes, through the usual channels. The industry was satisfied and the British government was satisfied.
Later there were changes in Great Britain. The private buyers or distributors ceased operations, and the British government took over the control of sales of fish and other foods through the food controller. Then we asked what service this government could render to the British government through the food controller, and we were told that he would continue to buy through the ordinary established channels, which had been found satisfactory. Recently we were informed that the British people would require a larger quantity of canned fish because of the fact that, owing to lack of shipping facilities and the difficulty of handling on the other side, they had to stop the importation of frozen fish, such as frozen halibut and salmon and cod or fish of the cod family, which had been imported in large quantities. Information was asked of the Canadian government through the usual channels, and the department was requested to supply the information. We were told that it was possible that the British food controller might require a much larger quantity than usual. Therefore, in order to give correct information, the deputy minister was asked to go to the Pacific coast to meet those interested and to find out to what extent the pack could be increased without impairing the future supply. The deputy minister met the packers and the fishermen in private meeting and got the information required, and we passed it on to the British authorities. There our negotiations ended so far as the department is concerned.
Did they say anything about prices?
Yes, naturally we ascertained the prices that the industry would demand for the coming season.

By "the
industry" the minister means the canners?

I mean the canners and the fishermen, because they are both part of the industry. The best information we could get was communicated to the British government and the food controller. Whether we shall be asked to act in any capacity we do not know. For that reason it is impossible
Supply-Fisheries

to give any more information than I have given. This statement appearing in the press did not emanate either from the department or the deputy minister, because the meetings between the deputy minister and the different branches of the industry were private meetings, closed meetings, and all that has appeared in the press as to what took place are surmises.
The hon. member for Comox-AIberni brought the matter to my attention on April 28 as reported at page 2303 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. A. W. Neill (Comox-AIberni): I should like to ask the Minister of. Fisheries a question. It is reported in the Canadian Press that the Vancouver Daily Province of April 24 carried a story that the major reason for the visit to Vancouver of Doctor Finn, the deputy minister, was the proposed acquisition of the entire British Columbia salmon pack by the Canadian government. This of course is a very important matter for the province, and I would be glad if the minister could make a statement.
And I replied:
Hon. J. E. Michaud (Minister of Fisheries): The hon. member for Comox-AIberni (Mr. Neill) was good enough to give me notice of the question. A little while ago we were informed that the food ministry of Great Britain would likely need, during the next production year, a much larger supply of canned salmon from Canada than it is customary for the industry to put up. The reason therefore for the recent visit to Vancouver of the Deputy Minister of fisheries was, first, to ascertain the possibilities of increasing the canned salmon pack to meet the requirements of Great Britain and, second, to study the best means of effecting its orderly shipment.
I am sure that if the British government ask the Canadian government to act as its agent or in any capacity to help to produce a larger supply of fish food for the British people, every facility will be offered. The cooperation of the government and of the Department of Fisheries has been assured from the very beginning of hostilities. If, in order to feed the British people, it becomes necessary to commandeer the British Columbia pack, I am sure the government would not hesitate to do so if the British people require it in the present crisis.
The question of the reduction of herring is one that has been discussed for years. Some people on the Pacific coast have thought it almost immoral to use fish for anything other than food purposes. Others have felt that the reduction of herring to produce fish meal and fish oil was detrimental to the salmon industry because it took away the food of the salmon. Others have thought that while the fish are there, advantage should be taken of their presence, and they should be used for the production of fish meal and oil, two FMr. Michaud.]
products which are in great demand. As hon. members are aware, fish oil is very much in demand and prices are fairly high. Fish meal is a product for which the demand is increasing every day, and it is used to produce other food products when fed to poultry, cattle and so forth as a protein food. The department has tried to satisfy both factions, and for years has established quotas in connection with the quantities of herring that could and should be reduced. Some people thought those quotas were too high; others thought they were too low, but every precaution was taken to maintain a proper supply of food for the salmon and at the same time meet the market demand for fish meal and oil.
The canning of herring on the Pacific coast has been started only since the outbreak of war. There was no canning to amount to anything before the war, but since then large quantities of herring have been canned and shipped to foreign markets, and to Great Britain; and probably, while hostilities continue, there will be a great demand for that product, having regard to the difficulties that exist in getting food to Great Britain. Therefore it seems that their requirements of canned fish of all kinds will continue to be large, and the Canadian industry is making every effort to make sure that it will have the necessary quantity to meet that demand.
Has the quantity been increasing in the last two or three years?
Yes, very much. Last year 8,000 tons of canned herring were put up and sent to the United Kingdom. That is a large quantity.
There could have been 18,000 tons if they had not been fished out in years gone by, for reduction purposes.
I suppose that is possible. This year, based on the information and inquiries already received, we believe the quantity will be much larger.
That is, assuming the fish are available.

Provided, of course, the fish are available. Before the war there was no demand on the Pacific coast for canned herring; the demand was for fish meal and oil, and the industry did the best it could under the circumstances, with the limited quotas that were available. I think there will be very little, if any, herring reduced during the coming year because of the great demand for canned herring, which has to be put up whatever the cost, even though the return

Supply-Fisheries
may be lower than would be the situation if the herring were reduced to fish meal and oil. Therefore I believe the present situation will cure itself, due to the great demand for canned herring for export.

I should like to finish my remarks. In large part the minister has corroborated what I have said; there is more money in canning herring-more money for British Columbia and for Canada-than in reducing them. You do not need to fish them all out; there are enough left. The minister spoke of putting on quotas. Yes, they did put on quotas in different areas. I recall one place where this was done; I forget whether it was Barkley sound or the area immediately west of it, but that is immaterial. When they put on the quota they also inserted a provision that if the fishery official thought too many fish were being taken, having regard to spawning and so forth, he could stop the fishing; and he did stop it when only 18 per cent of the quota had been taken. That was the action taken by the official, impregnated though he was with the view of the department that it was a good thing to reduce herrings; he was compelled to stop the fishing for that purpose in that area when less than a quarter of the quota had been taken. That may give the committee an idea of how wide of the mark the officials were in setting the quota, or it may be that the herring suddenly fell short of it.
As I said before, herring do not produce a profitable amount of fish oil and meal; it is only as a sort of hangover of the pilchard industry that it is profitable. The minister said there was a great demand for fish oil. That is true; but it is only true in time of war. In time of peace there was little sense in reducing herring; not only was it barely profitable to do so, but when you increased the supply you reduced the price. It was a rather tricky market; if you produced too much, the market went away down.
I should like to mention just two other points with which I forgot to deal before. In accordance with this same policy of giving a quota to anyone who wants it, a year ago and again this year the department have allowed the reducing of anchovies. This might well be a profitable industry with a little care and encouragement; they might be used to make sardines, or something like that. They never have been used for anything at all, and the government, perhaps rightly, said they could be reduced. I think that was a mistake. There was a possibility that we might have made an industry of the canning of these anchovies. But then another 14873-199
factor appeared. These anchovies are naturally small fish. I suppose they are three inches long, or somewhere around that. They had to be caught with a particularly small net. What was the result? Enormous quantities of young pilchards were caught. Millions, rather than hundreds of thousands of them were taken, because the net was so small that the little pilchards could not get out. Therefore, in their anxiety to catch anchovies and to make fishmeal of them they adopted this system which ended in the taking of enormous quantities of small pilchards, for which there was no need.
I listened to the minister's remarks about the visit of the deputy to British Columbia. There is a considerable misunderstanding somewhere. I hold in my hand an editorial in one of the fishing journals on the west coast, and I find in big letters the word "misrepresentation." Then it goes on to say, as I have said, that Doctor Finn himself would not deny that the canners and fishermen were asked to submit a slate of prices to the government in four days from the time of his first meeting, and by working night and day price lists were submitted. That seems to indicate that some action was going to be taken. The idea was "You get your price, and you get your price, and we will try to get them together, submit them to Great Britain, and something will be done." Then the editorial goes on to say that while these negotiations were going on, practically the same negotiations, or negotiations of a similar nature, were being carried on in the United States, and resulted in a huge sale of canned sardines. Apparently the same policy had been adopted there. Somebody from Great Britain was sent out, and the result was a huge purchase of sardines in the United States. Then the editorial goes on to say:
The question now arises as to how we can possibly continue to operate as a potential source of canned foodstuffs for the British people while we are to receive no assistance to protect the living standards of our own British Columbia men and their families. It is to be hoped that the disturbed and confusing situation now confronting us will be cleared away very shortly, and definite guarantees made to the fishermen before the season commences. So far, Doctor Finn's visit to the coast has certainly not had the effect that was expected of it and has done nothing to enhance the federal department of fisheries in the eyes of the fishermen.
Of course that is a matter of opinion, but I believe some effort should be made to clarify that situation. Something should be done to remedy this situation in the future. Try to get these people together-because apparently the original idea was to make some deal. That was a proper and natural thing to do. When the British government were no

Supply-Fisheries

longer willing or able to buy from the Japanese they would take a large proportion from us. Surely the best way to do this would be at a definite price. Cut out the middlemen, and the expenses for advertising, brokerage, labelling and so forth. Then both parties can sell profitably at a lower price. It will be better for the British purchaser and better for our own Canadian people.

What was the exact object of the deputy minister's visit to the Pacific coast? My second question is: did or did not the British government decline to deal with the dominion government, and express a preference to deal with private enterprise ?
There is no mystery, contradiction or conflict in this matter at all. We were asked if the Canadian industry could supply a much larger quantity of canned fish.
Asked by the British authorities?

Yes, through the usual
channels.
What are the usual channels?

The Department of
External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce. In order to give that information we had to meet the fishermen and the packers. We thought the best way to do it was to have a person in authority interview and talk with them, because the information was wanted within a few days.

That was
as to the question of supply?
Yes.
And price.

Price and quantity; we desired full information. When we ascertained from the packers what quantity they could put up, without adding additional equipment to their plant, and basing their figures on the prospect of this year's catch, the deputy asked them what their price would be. In order to get a definite reply the packers had to deal with the fishermen to find out at what prices the fishermen would sell their fish. They were told to get together, because we wanted the information. The deputy returned within a few days with the information which had been given to him, and that information was passed on to the Department of Trade and Commerce, the department of government which had asked us for the information. That is all there was to it. Then we were told it would be better for the government to commandeer the whole

pack. That would be a big job, because it is a S30.000.000 industry. In the past it has operated with a fair degree of satisfaction to both fishermen and packers, and has been worked along ordinary business principles. We are not at all anxious to step in and take charge of a large industry which in this year should be worth about $35,000,000. Further, we are not going to step in until we are told that we must do so, or until we are satisfied that it cannot run on its own feet. That is the present situation.

Has the
minister considered putting a floor on the price the fishermen are to receive? That has been done in respect of other products. Is there any complaint about the incomes of the fishermen?

So far there is none.
So far no representations have been made to us that the fishermen are not going to get enough. Of course there are some who may claim that they should get more, and that whatever the British government is willing to pay, the fishermen should get what they think they ought to get out of it. The same applies to some canners. They will say, "Our cost of operation is going up, and the British government is not willing to pay enough to meet our costs, plus a fair margin of profit." It is urged, therefore, that the Canadian government ought to supplement the price. We have not given any thought to an appropriation of public money to supplement the difference between what the packers ask and what the British government will be willing to pay. So far we do not know what they will pay.
The minister would not go on record seriously as saying he is convinced that the fishermen are satisfied with the prices they have received in the last two or three years?
Some are, but some are not satisfied, and never will be.

I think the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is a most important one. Last year at the beginning of the salmon season in British Columbia there was a dispute between the fishermen and the canners which held up fishing operations for a considerable time. I imagine the pack was not as large as it otherwise would have been if the fishermen had gone out when the season opened. I suggest that we ought to give consideration to this matter so that a food supply as important as salmon, and so great a factor in the economy of British Columbia, will not be held up this year. Let us not have the same situation as developed last year. It will be recalled that, before the

Supply-Fisheries
winter was over, there was a good market at a good price, which permitted the canners and packers to make a very good profit. The Department of Fisheries and the government should be prepared to take a chance. It is not a big chance, because salmon is a valuable food at any time. Certainly in our war economy $35,000,000 is not a great sum. We must remember that we are operating in a war economy, and the government should have a plan prepared so that when the fishing season opens, every fisherman will be able to go out fishing. I think the minister should take that into consideration and assure the committee to-night that a plan of that kind will be put into effect.

The relations of the fishermen with the packers under ordinary circumstances are a matter of provincial concern, not federal. Provincial laws have been enacted to establish and adjust the relations between the fishermen and the packers when conflict arises between them. We cannot treat present conditions as a war emergency because there is apparently a good market for the output of the industry, and any interference between the different interests under ordinary circumstances only makes for disturbance and disorganization without any beneficial results. I believe that these people can adjust their difficulties among themselves, and if they cannot, there is the machinery of provincial laws to assist them in adjusting their difficulties.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the request of the leader of the opposition I will tell the committee briefly what in my opinion is the situation both of the fishermen and the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast.
First of all, the war has had some good and some bad effects on the fishing industry as on other industries, but the effects of the war on the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast have been beneficial in this respect-

Beneficial?
315S

Beneficial in this respect, that they have eliminated a number of people who were classified as fishermen because they had no other occupation but who were fishing for only a few weeks of the year and who *were expected and who expected to live twelve months of the year on a few weeks' work in an industry producing low returns. They had poor equipment, and they were interfering with the legitimate fishermen who in the past had made fishing a calling, had made some kind of livelihood at it and had worked hard at that calling. On the Atlantic coast, with a few exceptions, the fishing season lasts from three to five months of the year at most. Outside of a very much limited number, the people who call themselves fishermen, and who are classified as fishermen fish for no more than five months of the year.
What the minister is saying is that there is very little winter fishing.

There is very little winter fishing. In the past, many people depended for their existence upon the returns of five months in the year; they were supported for the remainder of the year by people who allowed them just enough to keep them alive. That is about the situation. In some sections -of the Atlantic coast there were so-called fishermen who never saw real money until we distributed some relief among them.

That is
& pretty serious statement.
We have statements from fishermen to that effect.
All truck?

All truck, barter. They
were w'orking for three or four months in the year, or at most five months, dropping the products of their work into the warehouses of the dealers, getting credit on the books for the weight and quantity of fish, and receiving from the dealers a few bags of flour, a few gallons of molasses, sometimes lard-never butter-and enough clothing to keep the body covered. That is the most that the majority of them were getting. That went on for some time.
Then came the depression and prices tumbled, markets disappeared. The reserves of many years, sometimes generations of work, were in the hands, not of bankers, but of people who had invested in property, or sometimes, after dealing on the stock exchange, lost everything. All the reserves of the fishermen had gone, and they had to resort to relief. Consequently the situation had to be changed.

Socially-minded people were made aware of the conditions and became interested in the fishermen. Many suggestions w'ere put forward, but I believe the best which was offered was that the fishermen should be educated to look after themselves, to cooperate, and to try to become independent of those who had failed them in the past. That work was started by the fishermen and by the extension department of the St. Francis-Xavier university of Antigonish, Nova Scotia, who have been carrying it on now' for ten years.

As a
cooperative movement?
As a cooperative movement.
Good.

Recently that movement has been supported financially to a limited extent by the government, also by socially-minded private citizens, people of wealth in the maritime provinces and outside Canada, who make it their duty each year to collect sufficient funds to pay the costs of the work of the extension department of St. Francis Xavier university.

That is
educational?

Educational, yes. With
regard to the economic aspect, of course many people are finding more profitable employment in war work and have quit the fishing industry. This makes it more advantageous to those who are in the industry as a vocation; the market available to each fisherman is so much larger. Also, the price of fish has been increased through many factors. There is a bigger demand from the United States market and better prices are being paid. Also the home market has expanded and the prices have improved.

Just on
that point-the minister is making a general statement-what is the increased domestic consumption of Canadian-caught fish, this year, we shall say, compared with last year? Has he the figures?

We have figures on the
general increase of fish consumption in Canada, and it is our estimate that within the last five years the consumption per head has increased from seventeen pounds to twenty-eight pounds.

Does that include importations from the New England states?

We have no fish importations of any account from the New England states.

Where
does this so-called sole which we have at the hotel, come from?

It comes from the
Atlantic ocean, through-
I know.

-through Canadian
fisheries.
What part?
From the Grand banks, from the fishing banks, to which Europeans used to resort to get their supplies of fish.
There is no importation of fresh fish into Canada, then?
No, not to any extent.
Good.

There was some importation in the past of canned sardines from Norway and of pickled herring from Holland, the latter in very small quantities. Of course, all this has ceased. Take the increase in the exports to the United States; is that raw fish, or processed fish, or cured fish, or what?
It is processed fish. It is frozen fish.
Chilled?

Chilled, and frozen; but mostly frozen. It is pretty hard to place chilled fish with the exception of lobster, on the United States market. It is mostly fish treated by the modern process called "quick freezing".
Fillets, or whole fish?
Fillets.
Altogether?

Oh, yes. Another factor, besides the increased consumption both on the United States and Canadian markets, is that Norway and Newfoundland, both of which were competitors of the Canadian fisherman, have been eliminated as such, Norway wholly
and Newfoundland in part. Therefore the Canadian industry has less competition and a chance to dispose of larger quantities of fish, and naturally it gets better returns.

Has the export to the United States of fish taken in internal waters
increased ?

White fish from the
interior of Canada?
Winnipeg gold-eye, lake trout and so forth. .

We are maintaining our average, and the large increase is on the Pacific coast in frozen halibut, fresh halibut, frozen and fresh salmon, and on the Atlantic coast, cod products, haddock and lobsters.

The export of internal
fish is not dropping?

No; it is maintaining a stable market, which is fairly good in the middle states. There is not much interference on the part of other sections of the country with those markets in the middle states which are exclusive to inland water fish.
Is it advisable to increase production in the inland fisheries?
That is a matter of provincial concern. The provinces have control of their fisheries, which they regulate pretty well.
What is the plight of the codfish industry, which was once the back-bone of the whole industry?
We have had competition from Norway and the other Scandinavian countries which we had not before the first war, and there is competition from Newfoundland.
Which we have always had.

Yes, in a lesser degree, because they were not subsidized. When the British government began to subsidize the fisheries of Newfoundland they could compete with our fishermen, with the result that they invaded our best markets. Our industry was not subsidized. The same applies to competition with Norway, which was highly subsidized. After the last war they used their fishing vessels to full capacity and came into close competition with our fishermen, and they also invaded our markets. This competition from Norway and Newfoundland was the main reason for the falling down of our salt-fish industry. Conditions are, however, getting better. The monthly reports from our trade agents everywhere are optimistic. Orders for
